source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
finding: Meehl (1954) said proper linear models beat clinical judgment. Dawes says the literature since then supports it. He found no study where clinical judgment clearly beat a model.
numbers: Meehl (1965) knew of one possible exception; Goldberg (1968) disputed even that one. Sawyer (1966) reviewed many studies.
limits: Mostly psychology criteria with modest reliability. Holt (1970) criticised details of several studies.
agent_relevance: Prior for S7: when features can be scored, a fixed rule should combine them, not the model.

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
finding: Equal weights on GRE, GPA and school selectivity predicted later faculty ratings better than the admissions committee did.
numbers: N=111 Oregon psychology grad students. Equal-weight composite r=.48 with faculty ratings; committee judgment r=.19; cross-validated regression R=.38. Ratings reliable (variance ratio .67).
limits: One school, one criterion, rated by faculty who chose to rate. Both correlations are low.
agent_relevance: An unweighted sum of scored features can beat expert holistic judgment. Cheap to implement in code.

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
finding: Bootstrapping: a linear model of the judge's own past judgments predicts better than the judge. The model removes the judge's unreliability.
numbers: Wiggins and Kohen (1971): models of every one of the Illinois judges beat the judges predicting first-year GPA (90 students, 10 cues). Goldberg (1970): bootstrapping worked for 26 of 29 clinicians predicting neurosis vs psychosis from MMPI.
limits: One published exception: Libby (1976) loan officers (77% of 43 officers beat their models), reversed by Goldberg (1976) after rescaling skewed ratios (72% of models beat judges).
agent_relevance: Supports code applying the model's own stated weights consistently: consistency alone adds accuracy.

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
finding: Random positive weights also do well (Dawes and Corrigan 1974). So the sign of each cue matters more than its exact weight.
numbers: Dawes Table 1 compares judge, judge-model, random model, equal weights, regression and optimal linear model over five studies; in the GPA studies judges scored about .28 to .33 and equal weights about .34 to .60. The table text was garbled in extraction, so exact cells are not recorded.
limits: Needs conditionally monotone cues (each cue higher means criterion higher regardless of other cues). Fails for configural or non-monotone cues.
agent_relevance: Do not spend model calls tuning weights. Choosing which features to score and their direction is where model knowledge helps.

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
finding: Humans are good at knowing what to look for, bad at integrating it. Chess masters and expert doctors pick cues well but combine them poorly.
numbers: Einhorn (1972): doctors' overall severity ratings of Hodgkin's biopsies did not predict survival in 193 patients, though their coded features did.
limits: Single illustration studies.
agent_relevance: Directly matches S7 design: the model scores features, code combines.
quote: It is not in the ability to integrate information that people excel

source: Dawes (1979) The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making
finding: Simplest improper model beats judges on bankruptcy: ratio of assets to liabilities.
numbers: Libby task of 60 firms: loan officers got 74% (44.4 firms), their models 72%, assets/liabilities ratio 80% (48 firms); Beaver and Deacon linear models about 78% cross-validated.
limits: One small task; the ratio was chosen by the author.
agent_relevance: Simple single-cue rules are a strong baseline to test our agent's combined output against.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly & Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: a meta-analysis
finding: Across work and school criteria, mechanical combination of predictors beat holistic expert combination. Not corrected for range restriction, so true gaps are likely larger.
numbers: Job performance mean validity .44 mechanical vs .28 clinical (more than 50% better prediction). Advancement .42 vs .36. Training .31 vs .16. GPA .58 vs .48. Other academic criteria .47 vs .46 (clinical N only 161).
limits: Mechanical values use multiple Rs, which are upward biased; with the strictest shrinkage the mechanical edge was eliminated but not reversed on two criteria. No correction for unreliability.
agent_relevance: Largest recent confirmation in a hiring-style task, the nearest human analogue of an agent scoring items and ranking.

source: Kuncel, Klieger, Connelly & Ones (2013) Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: a meta-analysis
finding: Authors argue linear models are robust to weight changes, small samples are no excuse (use meta-analytic or aggregated expert weights), and expert-set weights still beat holistic clinicians.
numbers: Argument cites Dawes (1979). Uses the Brunswik lens model to frame judge vs environment.
limits: Discussion section, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Where no training data exist, ask the model for weights once, fix them in code, and apply them uniformly.

source: Ægisdóttir et al. (2006) The meta-analysis of clinical judgment project: fifty-six years of accumulated research on clinical versus statistical prediction
finding: Statistical prediction beat clinical, but the effect is small and consistent. Replicates Grove et al. (2000).
numbers: 67 studies, 92 effect sizes (173 with Goldberg 1965 and Oskamp 1962). Weighted d+ = -.15 (CI -.17 to -.13). Cross-validated studies, no outliers: 41 studies, 48 effects, d+ = -.12 (CI -.14 to -.09). Binomial display: 53% vs 47% right, called a 13% gain. Of 48 effects 52% favoured statistical, 38% no difference, 10% favoured clinical.
limits: Heterogeneous (Q significant). Small effect by Cohen standards. Studies from 1943 to 2004; clinical vs statistical.
agent_relevance: Calibrates expectations: gains from mechanical combination are modest on average and large only in some tasks.

source: Ægisdóttir et al. (2006) The meta-analysis of clinical judgment project: fifty-six years of accumulated research on clinical versus statistical prediction
finding: Boundary conditions: linear formulas helped; hand-built logical rules did not. Year of study, number of clinicians and number of predictions did not predict effect size. Criterion quality did not matter.
numbers: Linear formulas d+ -.15; logically constructed rules or signs d+ -.03 (CI included zero), Q_B(3)=11.94, p<.01. Criterion validity moderator Q_B(1)=.12, ns. No time trend (p>.05).
limits: Too few studies of mechanizing the clinician's own process for a test.
agent_relevance: Prefer weighted sums over hand-written if-then rules for combining scored features; rules matched clinicians.

source: Grove, Zald, Lebow, Snitz & Nelson (2000) Clinical versus mechanical prediction: a meta-analysis
finding: Mechanical prediction was about 10% more accurate than clinical on average. Advantage held across tasks, judge types and experience levels. Clinicians did worse when interview data were included. Effect d about .12 as quoted by Aegisdottir (2006).
numbers: Abstract-level only; I did not open the full text (study count from secondary sources not verified).
limits: Search abstract; the Aegisdottir text confirms d=.12.
agent_relevance: Interview-like free text inputs are where holistic reading hurts; keep S7 inputs structured.

source: Armstrong & Green (review of Tetlock 2005) Expert Political Judgment
finding: Summary of Tetlock (2005): experts barely beat informed non-experts, and neither group beat simple rules and models. In three-state questions forecasters often did worse than assuming equal chances.
numbers: 284 experts, 82,361 forecasts by 2003. Foxes (many ideas) forecast better than hedgehogs (one big theory), especially on long-range forecasts in their own area.
limits: Secondary review, not Tetlock's book. Politics did not predict accuracy.
agent_relevance: Forecast skill depends on method not credentials: argues for fixed procedures and many weak signals over one strong theory.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: IARPA tournament: top performers selected each year and placed in elite teams (superforecasters) did not regress to the mean over Years 2 and 3. Selection plus teaming beat training or teaming alone by a wide margin.
numbers: 60 superforecasters (top 5 from each of 12 conditions, 5 teams of 12). Years 2-3 average standardized Brier: supers -0.34, top-team individuals -0.14, all others +0.04. Resolution .40 / .35 / .32. Calibration .01 / .03 / .04.
limits: Volunteers (83% men, 64% some postgraduate study); status rewards not money; geopolitical questions only.
agent_relevance: Stable skill exists in forecasting; the best weights come from track record. Analogue: score components by past accuracy and reweight in code.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters as a method of improving probabilistic predictions
finding: Brier score definition and median-of-team scoring used in the tournament. Tracking was added at the end of Year 1 after Year 1 randomised trials found debiasing training and teaming each helped.
numbers: Example: p=.75 on the event that occurred, .25 on the other gives Brier .125 (two-category sum, range 0 to 2). Team score = median of individual scores. Minimum 25 forecasts earned a $150 gift certificate (Year 1), $250 (Years 2-3).
limits: Two-category Brier (0 to 2) is twice the binary (0 to 1) scale used in LLM papers: do not compare numbers across.
agent_relevance: Use a proper scoring rule as the agent's own self-score when it has forecasts to check.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament
finding: Year 1 and 2 randomised conditions: probability training, teaming and tracking each improved calibration and resolution.
numbers: Abstract-level only (page text not retrieved).
limits: Not opened; figures for the size of each lift not recorded.
agent_relevance: Training in reference classes and averaging is cheap to copy into a prompt template.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig & Mullainathan (2017) Human decisions and machine predictions
finding: Large modern test of the Meehl claim. A gradient-boosted tree trained on defendant records beat judges on bail, using quasi-random judge assignment to handle selective labels.
numbers: NYC data: 554,689 cases (80/20 split, 443,751 train, 110,938 holdout). Same jail rate: crime down up to 24.8%. Same crime rate: jail population down 42.0%. Riskiest 1% have 62.6% predicted crime risk, yet judges released 48.5% of them.
limits: Only released cases have outcomes. Judges may weigh other goals (race, crime type). Trained in one jurisdiction; national data gave similar results.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect persists with machine-learned (not just linear) models at scale. Selective labels warn about training on the agent's own past choices.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig & Mullainathan (2017) Human decisions and machine predictions
finding: Judges do not rank risk like the algorithm. Stricter judges did not jail the riskiest people first.
numbers: Had stricter judges detained in model-predicted risk order they would have jailed only 48.2% as many people or had a 75.8% larger crime reduction; actually they raised jailing 13.0 percentage points and cut crime 18.7%.
limits: Observational policy simulation; depends on contraction assumptions.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence of mis-weighting by experts, not just noise.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs forecast poorly. Retrieval, reasoning prompts and ensembling brought a system near the human crowd.
numbers: 14 LMs, binary questions from 5 platforms. Baseline best (GPT-4-1106) Brier .208; most models at or worse than .25. Full system Brier .179 (accuracy 71.5%) vs crowd .149 (77.0%) and crowd aggregate .146.
limits: Standard errors assume iid and likely understate error; Brier not comparable across question sets.
agent_relevance: Baseline for what a scaffold adds: roughly .03 Brier from retrieval and aggregation.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han & Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Where the system beats the crowd and where it loses: it wins when the crowd is uncertain and when many articles are found, and loses when the crowd is near 0 or 1 because the model hedges.
numbers: Crowd in .3-.7: ours .199 vs crowd .246 Brier. Selective forecasting under all three rules (crowd .3-.7, early retrievals, at least 5 articles): ours .240 vs crowd .247 (22% of forecasts, 43% of questions). Near 0 or 1: accuracy +7% but Brier worse by .04. Per platform: Metaculus-type and Manifold differ, e.g. Manifold .247 vs crowd .310.
limits: Selection rules derived on the validation set. Authors attribute hedging to safety training (hypothesis).
agent_relevance: LLM hedging costs Brier at extremes; code can recalibrate after the model scores (note G4: no extremizing votes).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park & Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: Median of 12 diverse LLMs matched a human crowd on Metaculus questions. Aggregation rescues weak individual forecasts.
numbers: 31 binary questions; 12 LLMs vs 925 human forecasters. LLM crowd Brier M=.20 (SD .12), beats .25 baseline t(30)=-2.35, p=.026. LLM crowd vs human crowd M=.19 (SD .19): t(60)=.19, p=.850. Equivalence found within medium-effect bounds (exploratory).
limits: Small question set; models queried at different times from the human crowd.
agent_relevance: Aggregating different models helps, but G4 warns samples from one model are not independent; use different models if voting.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park & Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: LLMs show an acquiescence effect: mean forecasts above 50% though resolutions split almost evenly. Showing the human crowd median improved both GPT-4 and Claude 2.
numbers: Mean prediction M=57.35 (SD 20.93), t(1006)=86.20, p<0.001 vs 50%. Exposure to human median improved accuracy by 17% to 28%, but simply averaging human and machine forecasts was better than letting the model update.
limits: Two models in Study 2; the human crowd median is external information the agent may lack.
agent_relevance: Check for yes-bias in any probability the model outputs; correct in code.

source: Karger et al. (2024) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Dynamic, contamination-resistant benchmark; best LLMs about at general-public level, clearly below superforecasters.
numbers: 1,000 questions sampled from a larger bank; 39 superforecasters surveyed. On the 200-item subset: superforecasters Brier .096, public .121, best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) .122. Full set: supers .076, public .096, GPT-4o .130; gap supers-GPT-4o .054, significantly larger than supers vs public.
limits: Human median per question; tables use different subsets so absolute values differ.
agent_relevance: Gives a target gap (about .05 Brier) a scaffold could be tested against.

source: Karger et al. (2024) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Extrapolated parity with superforecasters from model scaling trends, with wide uncertainty.
numbers: Log-linear fit of Brier on LLM Arena score: y=.506-.000298x (R2=.47); parity near Arena 1406 (bootstrap CI 1346 to 1633). On training compute: y=.844-.01213x (R2=.41), parity near 6.49e26 FLOP.
limits: Extrapolation from a few dozen models; large CIs.
agent_relevance: A rough yardstick, not a promise: scaffolds may shift the line without more compute.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on real-world forecasting against expert forecasters
finding: By mid-2025 the best reasoning model beats earlier human-crowd numbers but trails expert forecasters by a lot.
numbers: 464 Metaculus questions; o3 Brier .1352 (SE .0097), o3-pro .1386, GPT-4.1 .1542, o4-mini .1589, DeepSeek-r1 .1950, GPT-4o-mini .2743. Ten hired expert forecasters on 157 questions: mean Brier .1573, median .0225.
limits: Author warns Brier is not comparable across question sets; expert subset is only part of the questions; first draft called them superforecasters.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models improve forecasting strongly, so the schema should allow reasoning when it is used to score features.

source: Hsieh, Fu & Chen (2024) Reasoning and tools for human-level forecasting
finding: ReAct agents with search and numeric tools reached crowd-level Brier. Ensembling the agent helped; ensembling the base LM did not.
numbers: RTF ensemble Brier .169, accuracy 73.9% vs crowd .172, 73.8%. Ensemble of agents .169 vs single agent .180. Base LM (GPT-4o) ensemble .218 vs single .210.
limits: Small question set; base models other than GPT-4o were worse than guessing .5.
agent_relevance: Tool use plus code-side aggregation beats prompting alone; matches G5.

source: Ghaffarzadeh-Esfahani et al. (2024) Large language models versus classical machine learning performance in COVID-19 mortality prediction using high-dimensional tabular data
finding: On structured clinical data, trained statistical models beat LLMs that read the same data as text. Fine-tuning closed much of the gap.
numbers: N=9,134 patients, 4 hospitals. XGBoost and RF F1 .87 internal and .83 external. Best zero-shot LLM (GPT-4) F1 .43. Fine-tuned Mistral-7b recall 1% to 79%, F1 .74 external.
limits: One disease; classical models trained on the full labelled set.
agent_relevance: When labelled history exists, a code-side trained model beats model-as-judge for feature combination.

source: Can large language models logically predict myocardial infarction? Evaluation based on UK Biobank cohort
finding: ChatGPT and GPT-4 asked to give a 0 to 10 risk score from tabular risk factors discriminated poorly and chain of thought made them worse.
numbers: 690 participants resampled from 482,310. AUC ChatGPT .62 (CI .58-.66), GPT-4 .69 (.65-.73); with CoT .58 and .60. Decision tree .79, SVM .79, logistic regression .77, random forest .76. Open LLMs .60-.62.
limits: Small sample, prompt-only, older models; numbers converted to text.
agent_relevance: LLM holistic scoring of numeric features is weak; keep number combination in code.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree
finding: Intuition is trustworthy only where the environment is regular enough to learn and the expert had practice with feedback.
numbers: Abstract-level only, not opened.
limits: Not opened; no numbers captured.
agent_relevance: Sets the boundary: use holistic model judgment only for cues, not the final combination in low-validity domains.
